newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Angry Bulgarian townspeople block road to Greece.
newsitem.headline: Angry Bulgarian townspeople block road to Greece.

text.p: Angry citizens of a Bulgarian town, blaming their Socialist rulers for economic collapse, turned out in freezing cold to blockade road and rail routes to Greece for a second day on Thursday.
About 50 trucks are stranded in Doupnitsa, 60 km (37 miles) south of Sofia, and Wednesday's train to Thessaloniki was unable to get through and had to return to the capital.
Protesters, who turned out in shifts through the night, burned tyres to keep warm. An ambulance from the railway workers' hospital came out to join the blockade with a sign saying "No to misery."
"We are standing here in the cold for our children," said nurse Liliana Stoimirova on one of the barricades.
She said her son earned 12,000 levs ($11.75) a month as a doctor. "At the same time just one textbook for my granddaughter who is a student at the English language school costs 6,000 levs."
Shops in Doupnitsa did not open on Thursday and displayed signs saying "strike" or "protest." Groups of 20 to 30 young people marched round the town with flags, chanting anti-government slogans.
"We cannot afford to buy anything, even meat for our children. We can live without it but the children cannot," said Mitko Shopov, another protester.

Bulgaria has been plunged into its worst crisis since the end of communist rule in 1989 by 25 days of protests calling for immediate elections and an end to rule by the ex-communist Socialists, who won parliamentary elections in 1994.
Soaring inflation and the collapse of the national currency have eroded the value of salaries to the point where many professionals earn less than a dollar a day.

"My granddaughter is only five years old but we can afford to eat only beans every other day and this is not the best kind of food for growing children," said Liliana Shaleva. "I cannot even dream of buying her a chocolate bar."
The opposition stepped up strikes and rallies on Wednesday after the Socialists said they would form a new government.
Labourer Strahil Skoklyov said he believed many more people sympathised with the protest but were afraid of joining them.
"I think that the people are afraid to go out in the streets although they are humiliated. They are afraid because they know that the Socialists still have power," he said.
Doupnista police chief Dimitar Rasovski said traffic was completely blocked but the protesters had let through a couple of cars carrying children who needed medical treatment.

Not everyone in Doupnitsa was sympathetic. "I have been here since yesterday and I can't get out," said blockaded truck driver Emil Markov. "I am freezing to death and I cannot accept this form of protest."
